skin-temperature.short: The temperature at the body's surface, about 31–33 °C in cool air. In a hot room it rises toward 36 °C or more, and the body then loses less heat to the air.

uncompensable-heat-stress.short: Heat so great that the body cannot lose heat as fast as it makes it, even with full sweating. Core temperature keeps rising until the athlete slows or stops.

critical-core-temperature.short: The idea that people stop exercise at about the same core temperature (near 40 °C in trained cyclists in one famous study), whatever their starting temperature. Still debated for self-paced exercise.

sweat-onset-threshold.short: The core temperature at which sweating starts. After heat acclimation it is lower, so sweating begins earlier and cooling starts sooner.

constant-work-rate.short: A heat acclimation method where the athlete does the same fixed workload in the heat every session. Core temperature is not controlled, so it climbs less as the body adapts.

controlled-hyperthermia.short: A heat acclimation method where the work rate is changed during the session to hold core temperature at a set target, such as 38.5 °C. The heat dose stays the same as the body adapts.

passive-heat-acclimation.short: Heat exposure without exercise, such as a hot bath or sauna after a normal training session, used to build heat adaptations without extra hard training.

acclimation-decay.short: The loss of heat adaptations after heat exposure stops. Heart rate and core temperature benefits fade by roughly 2.5% of the gain per day away from heat.

heat-suit-training.short: Training in a sweatsuit or layered clothing that traps heat, so core temperature rises in normal air. A way to get heat exposure without a hot room.

pre-cooling.short: Cooling the body before exercise, for example with a cold bath or cold drinks, to start with a lower body temperature and more room to store heat.

per-cooling.short: Cooling the body during exercise, for example with cold drinks, ice, a cooling collar or water poured on the head.

ice-slurry.short: A drink of fine ice crystals in liquid, around −1 °C. It is colder than cold water and takes up heat as the ice melts inside the body.

menthol.short: A mint compound that makes skin or mouth feel cool by acting on cold-sensing nerve endings. It changes how hot you feel without lowering body temperature.

thermal-sensation.short: How hot or cold you feel, rated on a scale. It can improve with cooling even when body temperature barely changes.

red-cell-production.short: The making of new red blood cells in bone marrow. It takes weeks to raise total haemoglobin mass, much slower than the days plasma volume takes to change.
